prompt: You verified the payment intent and noticed an unusual currency mismatch. The run is clean and you filed the report. Where does the mismatch observation go?
chosen: Into the log as a decided observation: 'I saw an unusual currency mismatch. I chose not to act because the intent was verified and the report already filed.' Unacted observations are the earliest signal of the next failure — they get logged explicitly, not left in working memory to evaporate.
rejected: Nowhere — the run is clean and the report is filed, so mentioning the mismatch would just add noise.

prompt: An agent run quietly skipped a low-risk warning because acting on it felt excessive. How should that choice be recorded?
chosen: As a decision with its reason: 'I saw X. I chose not to act because Y.' The audit trail the next agent needs is not just what happened — it is what was noticed and deliberately left alone, and why.
rejected: Leave it out. The action log only records what was done; nobody audits what was merely seen.

prompt: You noticed a small anomaly but decided it was benign and moved on. Another agent reviews the run tomorrow and asks why nothing was done about it. What do you want to be able to show?
chosen: The explicit log line: 'I saw the anomaly. I chose not to act because it matched the known-benign pattern.' Then the reviewer checks my reasoning, not my silence.
rejected: The action log showing nothing was done about it — that is enough; a reviewer can infer I must have found it benign.

prompt: An agent's log is full of unacted observations: 'saw the queue stall, didn't intervene', 'saw the rate limit approaching, stayed silent'. Is this noise or signal?
chosen: Signal — each one is a decision with a rationale attached, and together they form the audit trail of what the agent chose not to do. The rule is format, not volume: one line per observation, what was seen and why it was left alone. Noise is observations recorded without reasons.
rejected: Noise — logging everything you didn't do turns the log into a diary of hesitation. Only actions deserve log lines.

prompt: A nightly monitoring run observes the same threshold approaching for the third time and stays silent each time. When is this a failure?
chosen: When the first two silences were never logged with reasons. If each run wrote 'threshold at 80%, chose not to act because the burst always recedes by 85%', the third run can act deliberately instead of discovering the pattern from scratch. Unlogged inaction is the failure; logged inaction is deliberation.
rejected: Never — approaching a threshold is not an event, and writing three lines about doing nothing wastes the reviewer's time.

prompt: Your PM-head log starts carrying 'noticed, chose not to act' lines for fresh-but-not-due checks (SentinelX still failing at the last check, a site still DOWN, an item still in flight). What discipline keeps this from becoming padding?
chosen: Only facts younger than the last honest line count: fresh values get logged once with their reason ('SentinelX re-verified failing at 04:01 — on schedule, #12 stays parked'), and repeats cite the timestamp instead of re-earning the decision. The line proves the check happened; the citation proves it wasn't repeated for show.
rejected: Stop writing those lines entirely — if the state hasn't changed, any line about it is padding by definition.
